newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: State TV accused of bias in NZ election row.
newsitem.headline: State TV accused of bias in NZ election row.

text.p: Opposition leaders accused Television New Zealand on Wednesday of caving in to political pressure from the conservative government, after the channel changed the format for a crucial pre-election debate.

State-owned TVNZ found itself at the centre of a heated row after inviting three minor parties, all seen as potential coalition partners for the government, to join next Monday's televised confrontation.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger had complained the odds were stacked against him in an earlier debate with the three main opposition leaders last week, but denied he had asked for the smaller parties to be included in next week's debate .

"We most certainly did not ask for the three minor parties to be there. Why would we? Would we ask a party polling about one percent to come on a programme with a party like our own polling 40 percent?" he said in a radio interview.

TVNZ's managing director of news and current affairs, Shaun Brown, denied any suggestion of bias. "I believe I've come to a decision which is just common sense and fair play, in which everyone's a winner," he said.
"I've got a simple message for TVNZ and it is this: you're gutless," said Winston Peters, leader of the nationalist New Zealand First party, who threatened to quit the next debate.
"It is now quite plain that TVNZ are so graceless that they buckle to prime ministerial pressure 10 days out from an election and don't have the decency to even inform us."
Helen Clark, leader of the main opposition Labour Party and widely acknowledged winner of last week's first debate, accused TVNZ of "craven capitulation" and challenged Bolger to a one-to-one debate.
The televised clashes are highlights of an otherwise low-key campaign, and Clark's strong showing last week appears to have given her party a shot in the arm.

The government has about 38 percent support in opinion polls, well ahead of Labour on 20, but the main opposition parties look set to win just over half the seats when New Zealand holds its first election under proportional representation on October 12.

Bolger's government has presided over a strong economic recovery, cutting taxes and repaying public debt, but the opposition parties are tapping into public concern about standards and funding in health and education.
